passage:
Trainee review note, week three

Siddharth joined the analytics team from a sales background. On Tuesday I gave him his first spreadsheet automation task. After an hour he came to my desk, red in the face, and said, "I can't do macros. I'm not a coding person." He sounded resentful, as if the task was unfair.

I asked him to change one word: "I can't do macros yet." He rolled his eyes but repeated it. Then I asked, "So what would you try next?" He thought and said he'd been copying code from forums without understanding it. We agreed a different strategy: record a simple macro, then read the code it produced, line by line.

By Friday he had automated the weekly report. He said, half laughing, "Still yet, for the hard ones." Next step: I'll pair him with Ravina for the database module.

— Sahil

qa.q: What did Siddharth say when he came to Sahil's desk?
qa.a: "I can't do macros. I'm not a coding person."

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when he first said he couldn't do macros?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and resentful, red in the face, as if the task was unfair and proved he wasn't suited to it.

qa.q: Why did adding 'yet' help only when paired with a new strategy?
qa.a: 'Yet' kept the door open, but it was the change from copying forum code to recording and reading macros that actually gave him progress.

qa.q: What would change if Sahil had only said 'just keep trying'?
qa.a: Siddharth might have kept copying code without understanding and stayed stuck, feeling even more that he wasn't a coding person.

grounding: It shows, through a supervisor's note, an adult who changes 'I can't' to 'I can't yet' and asks what to try next, with a better strategy making the difference.

passage:
Saturday

Failed the driving test again. Second time. The examiner marked me down for reverse parking, and I honestly felt like shouting at him. It was a tiny gap. Nobody could fit in that gap.

Came home and told Ritu didi, who taught me most of what I know. I said, "I just can't drive. Some people can't." She said, "Deepak, you can't reverse park yet. You can drive fine." That annoyed me even more. But then she asked what I'd been doing to practise. The truth is, I'd been driving around the colony, which I'm already good at. Never parking.

So what to try next? Ritu didi says there's an empty ground behind the temple on Sunday mornings. We'll put out two buckets and I'll reverse between them till I'm bored.

I still think that examiner was harsh. But okay. Yet.

— Deepak

qa.q: What did the examiner mark Deepak down for?
qa.a: Reverse parking.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel after failing the test?
qa.a: Deepak felt angry and resentful toward the examiner, and discouraged enough to say some people can't drive.

qa.q: What next step did Deepak and Ritu didi choose, and why is it a better strategy?
qa.a: Practising reverse parking between two buckets on an empty ground targets the exact weak skill, instead of more easy colony driving.

qa.q: How might Ritu didi see Deepak's 'I just can't drive'?
qa.a: Ritu didi probably sees it as frustration talking, since she knows Deepak drives fine and only needs practice at parking.

grounding: It shows an adult who shifts from 'I can't drive' to 'I can't reverse park yet' and plans a new strategy for what to try next.

passage: It was the last week of the quarter at the logistics firm in Pune, and every screen showed red numbers. There was no time to practise, no one to check her work, and last month someone had been shouted at for a small mistake. The poster suddenly looked silly. That evening, Wasim booked every Friday afternoon after the quarter as practice time on a test copy of the tool, with himself reviewing.

Dear Disha,

Three weeks at the law school. Everyone here seems to have debated since they were six, read every book, spoken at conferences. In the first moot court practice, a classmate quoted three judgments from memory. I just sat there.

I keep thinking the admission was a fluke. The entrance test that year had a lot of logic questions, which I'm good at. If it had been anything else, I'd be back home.

My first assignment came back with a good grade, and my first thought was, the professor must be marking easy for first-years.

Every time someone asks me a question in class, my heart races. I'm waiting for the day someone says, "Wait, how did you get in?"

You knew me in school. Did I ever seem like I belonged in a place like this?

Yogesh

Dear Santosh,

Four weeks in Delhi. The college is huge. Everyone talks about things I've never heard of: office hours, electives, internships in second year, CV. On the first day someone asked what my parents do, and when I said Appa drives an auto and Amma sells flowers, the girl just said "Oh," and turned away.

Last week I found a poster for a group of students who are first in their families at college. I went. There were thirty of us. A senior explained office hours: you just walk in and ask. I went on Tuesday. The professor was kind.

I still feel strange. But less alone.

Tell Amma I'm eating.

Your akka,
Yamini

September, first week. Pankaj stood outside the career centre at the university in Nagpur, holding his marksheet. First class. But inside, other students talked about "networking" and "online profiles" and "summer internships at big firms." His father farmed cotton; nobody at home had ever had an internship. He turned around and walked back to the hostel.

October, a Wednesday. Francis, a final-year student who ran a peer mentoring group for first-generation students, sat next to him in the canteen. "You looked lost at the career centre. I was too, my first year." He pulled out a sample CV and showed Pankaj how to write one.

December, a Monday. Pankaj walked into the career centre with a printed CV. He still felt his heart racing. But three other students from the mentoring group were in the queue, and one of them waved.

passage:
Monday night

Seema turned down the team lead role again today. Third time. In the meeting, when the manager announced it, she looked at the table the whole time. Afterwards I asked her why. She said, "I'm not leadership material. Others are more qualified."

I've sat next to her for two years. She's the one who fixed the billing error that saved the company from losing the biggest client. She trains every new joiner, patiently. In meetings she never speaks, but she sends the best ideas afterwards, by email, quietly.

I'm going to say something to her tomorrow. Not "you're great," she'll wave that away. Specific things. The billing fix. The new joiners. The emails.

I don't know if it will change her mind. But I think she doesn't see herself the way we see her.

— Reena

passage: Tushar, you think senior engineers never feel like frauds? Listen. At twenty-five I was the youngest designer on the dam project in Himachal. Every morning I walked onto the site sure that today someone would see I didn't know enough. I stayed quiet in meetings. I didn't sleep. One evening my mentor, old Mr Negi, found me checking calculations for the fifth time. I don't know why, but I told him. "Sir, I feel like I'm pretending." He laughed, not unkindly. "Anand, I've felt that on every project for thirty years. So has every good engineer I know." I nearly cried with relief. It was like a weight lifted. I still felt nervous the next morning, but the shame was gone. I could ask questions. That's why I'm telling you now, beta. Say it out loud to someone you trust.

"Can I tell you something embarrassing? I think I'm a fraud. Every day I'm waiting for them to find out." She felt her cheeks burn. Raghav didn't laugh. "I feel that every time I present to the board. My manager told me she feels it too. Apparently it's really common in people who are actually good." Sarita blinked. "You? You're the most confident person I know." "On the outside." When the train finally moved, Sarita felt lighter. The fear was still there, but it didn't feel shameful anymore.

qa.q: When was Sarita promoted to senior researcher?
qa.a: Two weeks earlier.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel after hearing Raghav felt the same?
qa.a: Sarita felt lighter and less ashamed, surprised that someone confident shared the same fear.

qa.q: What made talking on the stuck train helpful for Sarita?
qa.a: Saying the secret aloud to a trusted friend let Sarita hear that capable people feel it too, which reduced the shame.

qa.q: What is it like for Raghav to admit his own doubts?
qa.a: Raghav seems honest and comfortable sharing, perhaps relieved to talk about it too.

grounding: It shows an adult who tells a friend about feeling like a fraud and learns many capable people feel the same, which reduces shame.

passage: At the café near the Kolkata office, Jyoti stirred her coffee for a long time before speaking. Samir, her mentor, waited. "I got the grant," she said. "Everyone's congratulating me. And I feel sick. I think they made a mistake. I'm not as smart as the others." She stared at the table, ashamed. Samir leaned back. "Jyoti, do you know how many people I've mentored who told me exactly that? Almost every good one. I felt it when I got my first grant too." "You?" "Me. I thought they'd take it back." Jyoti let out a shaky laugh. The weight in her chest eased. "So what did you do?" "Kept working. Kept telling someone." She finished her coffee, and for the first time that week, she let herself feel a bit proud.

qa.q: What did Jyoti say she got?
qa.a: The grant.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel before and after Samir shared his experience?
qa.a: Before, Jyoti felt sick and ashamed, sure the grant was a mistake; after, the weight eased and she let herself feel a bit proud.

qa.q: What can Jyoti do when the feeling returns?
qa.a: She can keep working and keep telling someone trusted, as Samir suggested, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How does Samir seem to see Jyoti's fear?
qa.a: Samir sees it as common among capable people, not a sign that she doesn't deserve the grant.

grounding: It shows an adult who tells her mentor about feeling like a fraud and hears it is common, which reduces shame and improves her perspective.

passage: When I was ten, Abbu came home every Friday and asked one question: "How much in the test, beti?" If I said full marks, he smiled and patted my head. If I said eight out of ten, he just said, "Hmm," and turned on the news. One week I got six in maths. I folded the paper very small and hid it in my geometry box. For three days I felt sick every time Abbu looked at me. My cousin Vikas bhaiya found the paper. He didn't tell Abbu. He said, "Nazia, Abbu loves you, not your marks." I didn't believe him. I thought love was the smile, and the smile only came with full marks. Now I'm twelve, and I still flinch a little when someone asks about tests.

qa.q: Where did Nazia hide the maths paper?
qa.a: In the geometry box.

qa.q: Why did Nazia hide the six out of ten?
qa.a: She felt scared and sick, believing Abbu's warmth came only with full marks, so a low mark felt like losing his love.

qa.q: What could help Nazia feel loved beyond marks?
qa.a: Abbu could ask about other things, like what she enjoyed that week, and show warmth even after low marks.

qa.q: How might Vikas bhaiya feel finding the hidden paper?
qa.a: Vikas bhaiya likely feels sad and protective, wanting Nazia to know she is loved regardless of marks.

grounding: It shows a child whose father responds mainly to marks, feeling loved for performance and hiding a mistake.

passage:
Class 4 note, Thursday

Sabina got 7 out of 10 in the maths test. When I handed it back, she went pale and asked if she could take it home tomorrow instead of today. I asked why. She said quietly, "Mummy only smiles when it's ten. If it's seven she'll be sad with me." Later I found the paper in the classroom dustbin.

Sabina is a careful, bright child. The mark is fine. But she seems to believe that her mother's love depends on it.

I kept her back after school, told her that seven is a good mark and that mistakes are how we learn. I also called her mother this evening, gently, to share what Sabina said. Her mother was quiet, then said she hadn't realised. We'll meet next week.

— Sangeeta

qa.q: What mark did Sabina get in the maths test?
qa.a: 7 out of 10.

qa.q: Why did Sabina throw the paper in the dustbin?
qa.a: She felt afraid and ashamed, believing her mother would be sad with her and only smiles at full marks.

qa.q: What steps did Sangeeta take, and why were they helpful?
qa.a: Sangeeta reassured Sabina that seven is good and called her mother the same evening, so the belief could be addressed at home too.

qa.q: How might Sabina's mother feel after the call?
qa.a: Her mother may feel shocked and sad, not having realised how her reactions made Sabina feel.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child who believes her mother responds only to marks and so hides a mistake.

passage:
Friday

Rank card came today. Third in class. Papa looked at it and said, "Why not first?" Then he put it on the table and went back to his phone. He didn't say anything about my drawing that won the school competition.

At school Trisha said her mum hugged her for being tenth. TENTH. I didn't say anything.

I don't know. I think if I was first Papa would look at me longer. When I was first in Class 4 he took me for ice cream. I've been trying to be first ever since.

I hid the science worksheet where I made silly mistakes under my mattress. Mummy won't find it there.

I love Papa. I think he loves me more when I'm first though.

— Nikita

qa.q: What rank did Nikita get?
qa.a: Third in class.

qa.q: How does Nikita feel after Papa asks 'Why not first?'
qa.a: Nikita feels hurt and unseen, believing Papa's love grows with rank, so the mistakes worksheet gets hidden.

qa.q: What could Papa do differently?
qa.a: He could notice other things too, like the drawing prize, and show warmth whatever the rank.

qa.q: How might Trisha's mum's hug look to Nikita?
qa.a: It shows Nikita a different way, where love doesn't depend on rank, which makes the contrast painful.

grounding: It shows a child who feels a parent responds mostly to rank and hides mistakes, sensing love depends on performance.

passage:
A Tuesday in August. Vishal sat at his desk with the history project page. The first sentence looked clumsy. He erased it. The second try was worse. By midnight the paper had a grey smudge in the middle and a small tear. He threw it away and started a new sheet.

The Friday after. Still no page to show. His sister Zeenat found a pile of torn sheets under his bed. "Vishal, this is the fourth page. Why not just finish one?" "Because it isn't good enough." "Good enough for what?" He didn't answer. He didn't know.

The next Monday. The deadline came. Vishal handed in nothing. His teacher said, "Zero, then." At home, he stared at the torn sheets. "Even a clumsy page would've been better than nothing," he muttered. It felt like a stone in his stomach.

qa.q: How many pages had Vishal torn by Friday?
qa.a: Four pages.

qa.q: Why did finishing a page feel impossible to Vishal?
qa.a: He felt nothing he wrote was good enough, so finishing a clumsy page felt like failing, and he felt stuck and anxious.

qa.q: What could Vishal try next time?
qa.a: He could set a small goal, like finishing a rough draft first, then improving it, instead of aiming for perfect in one go.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel finding the torn pages?
qa.a: Zeenat seems puzzled and worried, seeing her brother struggle but not understanding why.

grounding: It shows a teenager who keeps erasing and rewriting until he hands in nothing, because finishing feels like failing, over several days.

passage: Zubin, you think I was always relaxed about work? Sit. In Class 10, in Surat, I had to write an essay for the inter-school competition. I wrote the first paragraph fourteen times. Every time, a word felt wrong, and I rubbed it out. The rubber went through the paper. I cried. My mother said, "Parveen, beti, send what you have." I couldn't. What I had wasn't perfect. The deadline passed. A girl from my class, who wrote hers in one evening, won third prize. I was angry at her, but I was angrier at myself. That night I understood something. My essay wasn't bad. It just didn't exist. Now, when I see you rewriting your science notes for the third time, I want to tell you: finished beats perfect.

qa.q: How many times did Parveen write the first paragraph?
qa.a: Fourteen times.

qa.q: How did young Parveen feel when the rubber went through the paper?
qa.a: She felt upset and helpless, crying because nothing felt perfect enough to send.

qa.q: What turning point in the story could have changed the result for young Parveen?
qa.a: If Parveen had followed the mother's advice to send what she had, the essay would have existed and been judged, instead of missing the deadline.

qa.q: How might Parveen's mother have felt watching her daughter cry over the essay?
qa.a: Her mother likely felt sad and worried, wanting Parveen to see that a finished essay was better than none.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a teenager, she rewrote the same page until it tore and missed the deadline because finishing felt like failing.

passage: The school's creative writing contest had a strict rule: forty-five minutes, one story, handwritten. Charu sat in the exam hall with the fan clattering overhead. She wrote the opening line. Crossed it out. Wrote it again. Rubbed out a word so hard the paper thinned. The invigilator called, "Twenty minutes left." Charu had three lines and a hole in the page. Across the aisle, her friend Hrithik was writing steadily, not stopping to fix anything. Charu tore off the page and started again. "Ten minutes." Four lines. Her heart was pounding. When the bell rang, she handed in a sheet with a title and half a paragraph. Outside, Hrithik said, "Mine's a mess, but it's done." Charu felt tears prick her eyes. His mess would be read. Her perfect first line wouldn't.

qa.q: How long did the contest allow for the story?
qa.a: Forty-five minutes.

qa.q: Why did Charu keep erasing and restarting?
qa.a: She felt anxious that nothing was good enough, so each flaw seemed unbearable and finishing a messy story felt like failing.

qa.q: What could Charu try next time the clock is running?
qa.a: She could write the whole story roughly first, then fix only a few lines at the end, so there is something finished to hand in.

qa.q: How does Hrithik see his own messy story?
qa.a: Hrithik seems relaxed, accepting that it's messy but proud it's done, which contrasts with Charu's fear.

grounding: It shows a teenager who rewrites the same page because it isn't perfect and ends up handing in almost nothing, as finishing feels like failing.

passage: Vandana, you ask why I'm happy when your drawings have mistakes? Let me tell you about my college years in Mysuru. Since primary school, everyone had said, "Chetan never makes a mistake." Neat notebooks, full marks, perfect projects. In engineering college, I kept it up. But I wasn't enjoying anything. I checked every assignment five times. When a friend asked me to join the robotics club, I said no. What if my robot failed in front of everyone? Then they'd see I was ordinary. In third year, I got one question wrong in a test, just one, and I couldn't sleep for two nights. My roommate found me at three in the morning, redoing the problem again and again. He said, "Chetan bhai, do you even like this subject?" I didn't know. I had only ever been afraid of losing it.

qa.q: What did everyone say about Chetan since primary school?
qa.a: "Chetan never makes a mistake."

qa.q: Why did young Chetan refuse to join the robotics club?
qa.a: He was afraid that failing in front of everyone would reveal he was ordinary, so striving was driven by fear, not enjoyment.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Chetan have begun to change?
qa.a: When the roommate asked if he even liked the subject, that question could have led him to notice the fear and try something like the robotics club.

qa.q: How might Chetan's roommate have felt finding him at three in the morning?
qa.a: The roommate may have felt worried and puzzled, seeing so much distress over one wrong answer.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a student praised for flawless work, his striving was fuelled by fear of seeming ordinary rather than love of the work.

passage: The design studio closed at nine, and Sahil still had the model on the table, with the jury the next morning. He had been praised all through school for perfect work, and in architecture college everyone expected his models to be the best. Tonight a wall of his foam model had a slight tilt, maybe two millimetres. His friend Jasleen said it was fine. "No one will see it." "I'll see it," he said. The watchman was locking up. He carried the model back to the hostel in the rain, covering it with his jacket, and rebuilt the wall until four. Jasleen texted, "Do you even enjoy this anymore?" He stared at the message. He didn't answer. The honest answer was no. He only knew he couldn't bear anyone seeing him as ordinary.

qa.q: What was wrong with Sahil's foam model?
qa.a: A wall had a slight tilt, maybe two millimetres.

qa.q: Why did Sahil rebuild the wall until four?
qa.a: He felt afraid that any flaw would show he was ordinary, so fear pushed him harder than enjoyment.

qa.q: What could help Sahil see his work differently?
qa.a: Letting one small flaw go at a jury and noticing that nothing terrible happens could loosen the fear, and talking to a mentor could help.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel reading Sahil's silence?
qa.a: Jasleen might feel worried and a bit helpless, sensing that her friend is driven by fear, not love of design.

grounding: It shows a student praised for flawless work who fears any mistake will reveal he is ordinary, so striving is fuelled by fear.

passage: Damini had been the topper since Class 1, and now, in her second year of economics at a Mumbai college, she was still getting perfect grades. Her friend Farhan asked her to co-write a paper for a student conference, something new and risky. Damini said no. "I'm busy." Really, she was scared. What if the idea failed? What if people saw that she was just good at exams and not truly brilliant? She stayed with safe assignments. At night she reread her old praise-filled report cards and felt a strange mixture of pride and dread. When Farhan's paper won a prize, she clapped, but her stomach twisted. She hadn't even tried. She realised she couldn't remember the last time she had enjoyed economics. She had only been afraid of not being the best at it.

qa.q: What did Farhan ask Damini to do?
qa.a: Co-write a paper for a student conference.

qa.q: Why did Damini say she was busy?
qa.a: She felt scared that a risky idea might fail and show she was ordinary, so fear of losing her image kept her away.

qa.q: What could Damini try to reconnect with enjoying economics?
qa.a: She could take one small risk, like helping with a section of a new paper, and focus on the ideas instead of the grade.

qa.q: How might Farhan see Damini's refusal?
qa.a: Farhan might think Damini is simply busy or uninterested, not knowing about her fear.

grounding: It shows a student always praised for perfect grades who fears any mistake will reveal she is ordinary, so her striving is driven by fear.
